newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's economy seen leading G7 nations.
newsitem.headline: Canada's economy seen leading G7 nations.

text.p: Low interest rates, stable inflation and strong economic fundamentals will propel Canada's growth rate past all other G7 countries in the next two years, according to a Reuters survey of economists.
The quarterly survey, which polled 27 economists in Canada and the United States, predicted the Canadian economy would grow by 3.3 percent in 1997 and 2.9 percent in 1998.
Canada's economy grew by 1.5 percent in 1996.
By comparison, the U.S. economy, which is running at full capacity, will grow only 2 percent this year and 2.9 percent in 1998, a companion Reuters survey in the United States showed.
The Canadian inflation rate was expected to be 1.9 percent this year, edging up to two percent next year, the economists said.
Last year, Canada's inflation rate was 1.6 percent.
Canadian growth would be driven by the great amount of monetary stimulus in the economy, said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Toronto-based Lehman Brothers Canada Inc.
"Interest rates are low historically and the Canadian dollar is significantly undervalued, both of which are providing a substantial degree of stimulus to monetary conditions," Gregory said.

The Bank of Canada has cut its key bank rate by 5 percentage points since May 1995. The bank rate, now 3.25 percent, is the top of the central bank's target range for overnight lending to financial institutions.
The bank rate determines prime lending rates by commercial banks, which are at 4.75 percent -- the lowest since 1959.
Economists have speculated in the past month that Canada's central bank would need to raise rates in line with a similar move in the United States.
The U.S. Federal Reserve raised U.S. interest rates by a quarter percentage point on March 25 in a pre-emptive move against signs of creeping inflation.

Officials at the Bank of Canada suggested in recent weeks that the country's improved fiscal situation gave the Bank more freedom than in the past to chart its own monetary policy. The current spread between U.S. and Canadian interest rates is 2.25 percentage points.
Most economists expect interest rates to jump by one percentage point in the next two years.

Gregory said that even an upward spike in the bank rate to 4.50 percent would only push the central bank's monetary policy into a position of neutrality -- one that neither contributes nor slows economic growth.
"From a longer term perspective, the real rate should roughly equal the rate of growth in the economy," Gregory said.
"If we're assuming 2.75 percent growth plus another 2.0 percent inflation, you're probably looking at 4.5 to 4.75 percent on nominal interest rates," Gregory said.
The expected rise in interest rates would relieve some of the pressure on Canada's dollar, which has taken a beating from worried investors this year.
Economists projected the Canadian dollar, currently at C$1.3977 (71.54 cents), would gradually strengthen through 1997, reaching C$1.3154 (76.02 cents) by the fourth quarter of 1998.
But not all survey participants shared the rosy outlook for Canada's economy.

Mark Mullins, chief economist with Midland Walwyn, predicted Canada was headed for a recession in 1998 because of rising interest rates, an inevitable slowdown in the U.S. economy and Canada's increasing dependence on international trade.
"Canada is more sensitive to any U.S. slowdown because trade now accounts for 40 percent of gross domestic product (GDP)," Mullins said. "In the late 80s, we were running at only 25 percent of GDP."
Mullins added the Canadian economy could not expect to keep benefiting from improvements in consumer spending, which have fuelled a huge boost in car sales and the housing sector this year.

"If there was a shock to confidence, if you saw a bit of a falling off on the export side, if you saw a bit of a tightening on the monetary side, you would have a more sensitive consumer," Mullins said.
